j.learned_fact: Library books are borrowed and must be returned so other children can read them; books are read front to back, page by page.
j.thinking_skill: connects her own action to its effect on someone else (returning the book lets the boy read it)
j.notes: The print-concepts lines ("You read this way, front to back") are bolted on and sound like a checklist rather than a child talking; nothing about turtles is actually learned despite the turtle book.

j.learned_fact: A pot cools down after the stove is turned off, and the steam stops — so it becomes safe to touch the side.
j.thinking_skill: links cause and effect (stove off → cooling, steam gone)
j.notes: The stray "onion seed rolled round and round" is an odd, unexplained detail that breaks the otherwise clean chain of cause and effect; also the story lightly implies touching a recently-hot pot is fine, which is a slightly risky safety message for a 4-year-old.

j.learned_fact: Smell contributes to taste: with a stuffy or pinched nose, food tastes bland; sniffing brings the carrot flavour back. Accurate.
j.thinking_skill: tests a variable (nose open vs. held shut) to explain a change
j.notes: The five-senses list is recited like a checklist, and the stuffy-nose/pinched-nose sequence is slightly confusing logic for a 3-year-old; sentence density and the implied experiment sit above JK level.

j.learned_fact: Red and blue mixed together make purple — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: observes a change and names its cause (mixing two colours)
j.notes: The final paragraph with the dropped brush is a bolted-on kindness beat unrelated to the colour discovery; otherwise simple, warm and age-appropriate.

j.learned_fact: Sinks have two taps: one gives hot water that can burn, and adding cold water makes it safe. (The line "Hot water comes first" is a quirk of that sink, not a general truth.)
j.thinking_skill: notices a cause and effect and states a simple rule from it
j.notes: Thomas's summarizing speech ("Hot water comes first. Cold water makes it okay") is more articulate and abstract than a three-year-old's, and it doubles as the moral. The cookie episode is a second, unresolved thread that dilutes the safety focus.

j.learned_fact: A zipper only closes when the pin end is pushed all the way down into the slot of the slider — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: inspects a stuck object and identifies the cause of the failure
j.notes: Nora's tidy explanatory line ("The zipper needs the slot... that is why") sounds more like an adult summing up the lesson than a three-year-old; "slot"/"slider"/"point" is slightly technical vocabulary for the band, though context carries it. Sheep pretend-play is decorative rather than integral.

j.learned_fact: A tablet that won't respond to a tap may need a long press on the power button to wake up or sleep.
j.thinking_skill: tries a new action after tapping fails, then links cause to effect
j.notes: Stray, illogical lines ("The bus was heavy and slow", "His coat would hang on the hook") break the flow, and the tablet is taken from a table but returned to a shelf; the self-question-and-answer at the end feels bolted on.

j.learned_fact: Taking turns means both children get to play; the rain/wheels detail teaches nothing and the claim that wheels "did not slip" on wet road is dubious and unexplained.
j.thinking_skill: notices that having the toy alone is not fun, so changes behaviour
j.notes: The window/rain paragraph is a dangling non-sequitur that neither causes the idea nor teaches a fact, and the closing "Because we take turns" states the moral flatly. Sentences are short enough for age 3, but the plot hinge is unclear to a toddler.

j.learned_fact: "Wild bears live in the woods" — true, but thin; the stronger learning is reading faces (down mouth, wet eyes = sad).
j.thinking_skill: reads another's face and revises her own angry reaction
j.notes: Emotion words are labelled rather mechanically ("Sara felt angry", "He felt sad"), and the ending lurches to an unexplained "Snack time at the store" that abandons the library setting and the borrowed book.

j.learned_fact: Sun warmth dries up puddles (simple evaporation), and the time words yesterday/today/tomorrow — "Tomorrow comes after I sleep."
j.thinking_skill: infers a cause (sun) for an observed change
j.notes: The yesterday/today/tomorrow vocabulary feels deliberately inserted, especially the stilted line "Tomorrow comes after I sleep"; the sock-sticking detail and ending are a little flat for a 3-year-old, who would want more sound, repetition and playfulness.

j.learned_fact: Cold butter is hard and tears toast; warming it makes it soft and spreadable. Also, pouring slowly prevents spills.
j.thinking_skill: identifies a cause and retests it after changing one condition
j.notes: Charlie's tidy conclusion sentences ("It ripped because the butter was cold") sound more like an adult narrator's lesson than a four-year-old; the stray "flower on the plate" detail goes nowhere. Slightly long sentences/paragraph blocks for a read-aloud JK listener, but concrete, familiar and warm.

j.learned_fact: A bigger breath blows out more candles than a small puff — a simple, true cause-and-effect about force of air.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect and adjusts her action
j.notes: Warm and age-appropriate, but the content is thin: counting three candles and one small discovery. The fork-returning bit is an unconnected add-on.

j.learned_fact: Hot things (like a grill just used for cooking) can hurt you, so you don't touch them; water in a puddle feels cold. The story's claim "the puddle is cold because it is water" is a false generalization — water can be hot too.
j.thinking_skill: notices a cause and effect (grill is hot because Dad cooked on it) and contrasts hot vs cold
j.notes: The hot/cold "lesson" is bolted on: Maria's tidy causal summary sentences sound like an adult's line, not a three-year-old's, and one of them ("cold because it is water") is simply wrong. A 3-year-old deliberately reaching toward a hot grill is also an unfortunate model.

j.learned_fact: Counting to six, and that taking two away from six leaves four.
j.thinking_skill: recounts a set after two items are removed and links the new number to the cause
j.notes: Pleasant and age-appropriate, but slight: the "counting song" is mentioned and never used, and the math content is thin (one count to six, one recount). Little narrative tension.

j.learned_fact: A stadium "wave" happens because people stand up one after another, in turn.
j.thinking_skill: notices a cause and effect (people standing in turn makes the wave)
j.notes: Warm and age-appropriate, but the ending line states the lesson a bit too explicitly for a three-year-old speaker; plot stakes are minimal and the counting motif is underused.

j.learned_fact: Waiting for your turn and sharing is kind — a social routine, not a fact.
j.thinking_skill: waits her turn; loosely links the boy's sharing to her getting an apple
j.notes: The stray line about cart wheels going "deep in the rug" is confusing and unrelated, and Emilia's closing line ("He shared, so I got my turn") muddles the turn-taking lesson. Sentences are otherwise nicely short for age 3.

j.learned_fact: The five senses pair with body parts: nose smells, ears hear, eyes see, fingers feel, tongue tastes. However, the claim that holding your nose makes the crunch of crackers "go quiet" is false — pinching the nose does not stop bone-conducted crunching sounds; it dulls flavour, not hearing.
j.thinking_skill: matches each sensation to its body part and counts them
j.notes: The central "trick" is factually wrong and confusingly written (five cups are promised but only three are described). For a four-year-old the game format is good, but the nose/ear muddle is the sort of thing a young child will remember incorrectly.

j.learned_fact: Taking and holding a big breath makes your body float in water (true—full lungs increase buoyancy).
j.thinking_skill: imitates a modelled action and repeats it to confirm the result
j.notes: Warm and simple, but slightly long with a few abstract touches ("a little shy") for a 3-year-old; story does not signal adult supervision in water beyond Mom watching.

j.learned_fact: Pouring slowly with the cup low on the table prevents spills; gentle taps spread butter better than hard pushing.
j.thinking_skill: adjusts an action after a failure and restates the cause-effect rule
j.notes: The "stormy sky / stormy milk" simile is an odd, abstract aside for a three-year-old, and Chloe's summary lines ("The cup stays still when it sits down") are phrased like adult morals rather than toddler speech; a knife for a 3-year-old is also questionable.

j.learned_fact: A shot is a quick pinch; counting to three and looking away helps it feel fast and less scary.
j.thinking_skill: connects a coping trick to her own feeling ("the count made it fast")
j.notes: Typo "bandade"; small logic slips (she "ran to the clinic door" eager for a shot, then is scared; she jumps "off the bed" though she was in a line). Simile "like noodles" is good but "jumpy tummy" is the only emotional detail developed.
